summary: Study done in about 48 minutes, stand-alone numpy only, nothing in src/ touched. Blunt verdict: the square pillow rule is NOT the answer for the Mandelbrot solid (a lopsided rock with fins, no bulbs, at power 2; a cushion with horned corners at power 3), and NOT for Julia sets with c on the real axis (c = -1 is one fused lump: cut at the touching point is a figure of eight, 21 % of the centre cut). It IS nearer than "Sphere inversions, one plane", the quaternion square and the Mandelbulb in one place only: Julia sets with c in the flat plane and off the real axis. There the rabbit is separate bodies that meet at single points with smaller bodies round them, and the power 3 Julia set for c = i is a ball with bodies on every side and round knobs on knobs at three sizes. With the layout in the brief the power 2 surface smears into one-way ridges and streaks at small sizes; a second layout I tried (Joukowski, closed form, no cubic) keeps knobs on knobs on the rabbit down to a box 0.01 wide but makes c = -1 and the Mandelbrot solid smoother. The property the rule was chosen for holds only without c: with c added, shapes are not kept under repetition (rabbit 12 to 1 after 14 steps, about the same as the Mandelbulb; c = -1: 2,700 to 1, far worse than the Mandelbulb's 12). The cut at z = 0 is the flat set point for point in every case tested. Deliverable: out/r15/study/sheet-for-user.png (plus sheet-layouts.png).

findings: MEASURED. The flat plane is exact: cuts at z = 0 match the flat sets point for point (Mandelbrot power 2 and 3, c = -1, rabbit, power 3 c = i: no grid point differs).

MEASURED. c = -1 is one lump, not bodies touching at points. The cut across the touching point is a figure of eight with 21.5 % of the centre cut's area (old table: one plane 3.8 %, old pillows 27 to 119 %). There is matter above and below the touching point for a height of about 0.54 each way, nearly as tall as the body itself. Near the point the outside reaches it only from the two y sides, in a double cone; the shape of that pinch is the same at three sizes.

MEASURED plus REASONED. Why: the rule keeps the upright plane y = 0 (the plane through the real axis and both seams; measured to 2e-16). Inside that plane, at power 2, the directions are folded onto half of the circle instead of going round it twice (measured: 181 of 360 degrees). So for real c the orbit of that plane never leaves it and behaves like a folded flat map, which gives a filled band. Reasoned, not tested for other real c: this should hold for every c on the real axis and for every layout that is mirror-symmetric left to right; all ten layouts I tried kept c = -1 in one piece.

MEASURED. The rabbit (c in the flat plane, off the real axis) is the good case: three bodies meet at one point (ball taken out: 3 pieces, at two sizes; upright line through the point is outside except the point), bodies are faceted, with smaller separate bodies round them. But lifting c 0.12 off the flat plane grows the bodies together (97.7 % in one piece).

MEASURED, by eye on voxel pictures. Detail at smaller sizes, layout of the brief, power 2: it goes on (surface stays 6 to 10 times rougher than a flat sheet at every size) but its kind is ridges, grooves and thin flakes that all run one way; at a box 0.01 wide on the rabbit only parallel streaks are left. That is smear, not smaller bodies.

MEASURED. Does it keep shapes under repetition? Without c yes: the shape error is steady, typically 1.9 to 1 at 1 step and at 6 (99 %: about 18). But the brief's expectation was wrong on two counts. (a) The Mandelbulb without c is also steady (1.43 to 1, lower than the pillow; only its tail is heavier, 99 %: about 50); only 'one plane' grows without end. (b) With c added the pillow's error grows with every step: rabbit 12 to 1 after 14 steps (Mandelbulb 10, one plane 85), c = (-1, 0.15, 0.1) 28 (Mandelbulb 46, one plane 2,010), c = -1 2,710 (Mandelbulb 12, one plane 906,000). So: far better than one plane, no better than the Mandelbulb, and worse than it on the real axis.

MEASURED. The layout matters a lot. A Joukowski layout (formula under needs_from_others) cuts the rabbit's number from 12.4 to 3.7 (height 1.0) or 3.1 (height 1.3), and its rabbit shows knobs on knobs at box widths 0.64, 0.04 and 0.01. At height 1.3 the rabbit's bodies still meet at a point (3 pieces); at height 1.0 they are fused round the meeting point (1 piece, 98.8 %). The price: c = -1 becomes a smooth lump with horns, the Mandelbrot solid a smooth rock with fins, the belt is no longer angle-true (sideways stretch just off the plane 1.5 to 2.5 at height 1.0, 1.74 to 2.26 at 1.3, instead of 2.00), and c = (-1, 0.15, 0.1) turns to dust at height 1.0 (volume 0.0017 against 0.81), so the Mandelbrot solid itself changes shape with the layout.

MEASURED. In the ellipse family of the brief: a shorter pillow (height 0.8) or a shorter seam (factor 0.35) improve the numbers a little (rabbit 9.4 and 9.7 against 12.4); a taller pillow (1.3) or a longer seam (0.65) are worse. Only seam factor 0.5 keeps the belt angle-true in that family (0.35 gives 1.72 to 2.60).

MEASURED. Mandelbrot solid, power 2, layout of the brief: a lopsided rock with fins and curtain-like folds, three times as much above the plane as below (1.54 against 0.52), reaching z = +1.69 and only -1.02. No bulbs. Its upright cut along the real axis is one filled blob with fins.

MEASURED. Power 3 (layout of the brief): mirror-symmetric to the voxel. The Julia set for c = i is the best-looking solid of the study, a ball with bodies round it on every side and round knobs on knobs at three sizes, and its shape error grows slowly (2.7 after 9 steps). The Mandelbrot solid at power 3 is a cushion with four horned corners and a plain rounded square as upright cut: no bulbs there either. Caution: c = i lies in a plane the power 3 rule keeps (x = 0), and I have no power 3 Julia set off the kept planes.

VERDICT, blunt. For the user's goal (a 3D Mandelbrot with detail in every direction) this rule is not it: the Mandelbrot solid is a rock at power 2 and a cushion at power 3, and the whole real axis is fused. It is nearer than one plane, the quaternion square and the Mandelbulb only for Julia sets with c in the flat plane and off the real axis, where it gives real separate bodies in every direction, and small bodies on them at power 3 or with the Joukowski layout. The entry's planned sentence 'double both ways on that grid and nothing smears' is not borne out with the brief's layout at power 2: it smears to streaks.

FOR THE ENTRY ENGINEER, MEASURED. The reference pillow_ref.py loses accuracy next to the seams, because its bisection fixes beta to an absolute 1e-18: within 1e-4 of a seam 2.8 % of directions are off by more than 1e-9 in the round trip (worst 1.4e-4), within 1e-5 26 % (worst 1.6e-2). On plain random points it is fine (five draws of 20,000: worst 1.8e-10). fastpil.py holds 4e-16 down to 1e-4 from a seam and 3e-9 closer.

needs_from_others: Orchestrator, decision for the user: the rule fails as a Mandelbrot solid and on the real axis, and works as Julia sets for c in the flat plane off the real axis. If the entry is kept, its texts should say exactly that, and should not say 'nothing smears' for power 2 with the brief's layout.

Entry engineer, if a layout dial is wanted: the Joukowski layout is cheaper than the cubic (one complex square root) and is the best I found by question 3's numbers and on the rabbit. Formula, power n, pillow height h (h = 1 square; I tried 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, 1.7; 1.3 kept the rabbit's bodies apart): t0 = h/(n+1); wN = h/2 - t0, wS = t0; aN = exp(-2 pi wN), aS = exp(-2 pi wS) (n = 2, h = 1: aN = 0.350920, aS = 0.123151). Sphere to pillow, unit d: a = aN if z >= 0 else aS; p = (x, y)/(1 + |z|); J = px (1 + a^2) + i py (1 - a^2); w = sqrt(J^2 - 4 a^2) with the sign that makes Re(conj(J) w) >= 0; zeta = (J + w)/2; s = arg(zeta)/(2 pi); te = -ln(clamp(|zeta|, a, 1))/(2 pi); t = t0 + te north, t0 - te south. D: u = (n t) mod h; u <= h/2: (-n s, u); else (n s, h - u). Pillow to sphere: north if t >= t0; rho = max(exp(-2 pi |t - t0|), a); nu = 2 pi s; p = ((rho + a^2/rho) cos nu/(1 + a^2), (rho - a^2/rho) sin nu/(1 - a^2)); d = (2 px, 2 py, +-(1 - |p|^2))/(1 + |p|^2). Checked in fastpil.py (class LayJ): round trip 1e-15, equator against angle doubling 9e-16 (power 3: 3e-15), no jump. It must be said in the text that with this layout the belt is not angle-true and that c = -1 and the Mandelbrot solid come out smoother.

Entry engineer, your check against pillow_ref.py: on random points it will pass at 1e-9 (I saw worst 1.8e-10 on five draws of 20,000), but any test point within about 1e-4 of a seam can differ by up to 1e-2 through the reference's own error. For a tighter reference import out/r15/study/fastpil.py: F(x, y, z, get_lay(REF)).

Entry engineer, for your close-ups and texts: the rule keeps the upright plane y = 0; expect c = -1 and every real c to be fused there, and the Mandelbrot solid's cut at y = 0 to be a filled blob. If your page pictures show something else, one of us is wrong and it should be looked at.
risks: All pictures and counts are voxel grids (321 or 257 a side for whole solids, 225 for close-ups, 40 to 110 steps). 'Separate pieces' and 'one piece' mean at that grid: joins thinner than a voxel are missed, bodies closer than a voxel are merged. The 3-piece result for the rabbit was repeated at two box sizes; the 97.7 % one-piece result for the lifted rabbit is at one grid only.

The words for the kind of detail (ridges, streaks, knobs) are my reading of voxel renders at one surface spot per solid. Dark flat patches in the close-ups are gaps or the walls of the box, I did not tell them apart.

The stretch numbers 'next to the surface' depend on the sample (random points that stay 16 steps and then leave; 600 to 24,000 points per case). For c = -1 with some layouts the sample is small (57 to 180 points), so those cells of q4-numbers.log are weak.
The comparison in looks with the Mandelbulb, the quaternion square and one plane is not from pictures made here; only the Mandelbulb and one plane were measured, and only for stretch.
The claim that the fused real axis is built into every mirror-symmetric layout is reasoned from the kept plane; it was observed for c = -1 in ten layouts, not proven and not tested for other real c.
The best-looking result (power 3, c = i) has c inside a plane that the power 3 rule keeps; I do not know what power 3 Julia sets look like off those planes.

A settle shortcut was used for the solids (an orbit that returns to within 1e-6 of its place 12 steps earlier counts as inside); on six test cuts it changed no point, but it was not tested on the Mandelbrot solid.

findings: The rule works as designed: no jump (400,000 close pairs, largest gap shrinks with the step), the plane z = 0 is exact, and the page's cut is the flat set pixel for pixel.

Power 2 does not give what the user is after. Mandelbrot solid: one lopsided rock with fins and a streaked, swirled skin. c = -1: a row of spiky bodies that stay joined (neck 24 % of the middle cut, against 4 % for one plane). Rabbit: lumps. c = i: a branching coral. c = 0.3: one smooth block.

Close up at power 2 (three depths, four places, and point-by-point cuts in 64-bit numbers without the picture's distance estimate): detail does go on at smaller sizes, but as streaked sheets, blades, thin slits and marbled swirls, like combed or stirred paint. No smaller bodies. The plain cuts show the same slivers, so the streaks are real, not a drawing fault.

The sentence 'double both ways on that grid and nothing smears' is not borne out at power 2. The grid is doubled evenly, but this layout puts it on the sphere unevenly: within 5 degrees of the plane z = 0 a small circle stays nearly a circle (5 % out of round), but over all directions the median stretch ratio is 1.64, about one in six directions is over 3, and 50 to 90 degrees north of the plane the median is 3.6. That this causes the streaks is my reasoning, not tested; the text says so.

The stretch falls to 0.001 beside the upper pole and reaches 10 beside the corner points in the lower half (300,000 directions, stretch_where.txt). The page's scorecard reads roundness 53 % at power 2.

Power 3 looked clearly better in the one place examined: the Julia set c = (0.3, 0.5, 0) shows buds with rings of smaller buds on them at camera distances 1 and 0.25, softer bumps at 0.06, no streaks; the point-by-point cuts show a bumpy outline with no slits (two small steps in it at the smallest size, not explained). The Mandelbrot solids at powers 3, 4, 5 are blocky bodies with knobbly buds on corners and rims, seen from the opening view only. Power 3 is mirror-symmetric above and below; 2, 4 and 5 are not.

The skin of the 3D picture can be trusted to about 0.05 (11 pixels of the opening picture) for the Julia sets tested, and about 5 in 6 stops are within 0.0125. That is close to Sphere inversions, one plane (0.025) and far better than the old Pillow (over 0.1 in places).

out/me/r15/pillow_ref.py is coarse within about 1e-7 of the plane y = 0: its 60 halvings stop near 1e-18 where beta itself is about 1e-16, which puts its answer off by up to 2.6e-3 there. Random points do not show it (2.6e-12).
